issues.legal_issue: A court may not sustain a defense on a materially new case that was neither pleaded nor consistent with the pleaded case.
material_facts: The defendants claimed that their possession arose from a permissive arrangement and denied that the sellers had any connection with the disputed shares.
The trial court nevertheless found that the sellers had granted a tenancy over those shares, although that case had not been pleaded and conflicted with the defendants’ pleaded position.
The High Court rejected that finding, and the Supreme Court found no basis to doubt the High Court’s conclusions.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was not justified in making out a new and inconsistent case for the defendants; the High Court’s rejection of that approach was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A court should decide the dispute on the cases made by the parties and should not supply a materially new case that was not pleaded. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_decree: A party appealed a civil court’s decree.
predicates.trial_court_relied_on_unpleaded_case: The trial court based its decision on a case that a party had not pleaded.
predicates.unpleaded_case_conflicted_with_pleaded_c: The case supplied by the trial court was inconsistent with the case the party had pleaded.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns a decree based on an unpleaded case that conflicts with the pleaded case, the decision cannot rest on that unpleaded case.

issues.legal_issue: A title holder may rely on permissive occupants’ possession as the title holder’s possession until the occupants assert possession adverse to that title.
material_facts: The plaintiffs purchased the disputed lands from the defendants who held title and sought confirmation of possession and recovery of possession.
The defendants in possession cultivated the lands as kinsmen of the title holders under a permissive arrangement, rather than as tenants.
The rent receipts supported acknowledgment of the title holders’ rights, and any assertion of adverse possession occurred only shortly before the sale to the plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs were challenged on the ground that they had not themselves been in possession within the relevant twelve-year period.
issues.conclusion: The defendants’ permissive possession was treated as possession through the title holders until an adverse claim was asserted, so the plaintiffs’ possession claim was not defeated merely because they had not personally possessed the lands during the relevant period.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the principle that a person in permissive possession is treated as holding possession for the person whose title is acknowledged, until the possessor asserts an adverse right. It relied on the finding that the occupants’ rent payments acknowledged the title holders’ rights. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_possession_decree: A party appealed a civil decree concerning recovery of possession.
predicates.claimant_acquired_title_from_title_holde: The claimant acquired title from a person who held title to the property.
predicates.occupant_possession_was_permissive: The occupant held and used the property with permission rather than under an adverse claim.
predicates.occupant_acknowledged_title: The occupant’s conduct, including rent payments, recognized the title holder’s rights.
predicates.adverse_claim_was_asserted_only_shortly_: The occupant asserted a claim adverse to the title holder only shortly before the property was transferred to the claimant.

issues.definition: When a claimant derives title from a title holder and the occupant’s possession was permissive and acknowledged that title until shortly before transfer, the claimant’s possession claim is not defeated by the claimant’s lack of physical possession.
